utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, two short matters before the witness returns. First, there was yesterday a notification that we would be seeking to change the order of the next two witnesses from C-007 -- sorry, from being Van Baal followed by C-007 to being C-007 followed by Van Baal. The reason for that notification was that we understood that if C-007 was detained until tomorrow as opposed to being completed today, there would be very substantial travel cost implications. In the event, when I checked the matter further, there are no significant implications. I'm sorry that that notification was given because it was avoidable. I don't know if either the amicus or the accused has made preparations based on the notification. We are happy to proceed with either ordering of the witnesses today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'd be grateful if these changes could be kept to a minimum. I understand there may be occasional logistic difficulties, but it does add very much to the strain on those involved in the case if there are changes of this sort. So the plan is that we hear Mr. Van Baal as originally notified and then C-007.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Indeed, unless the accused or the amicus, having received our letter yesterday, would now prefer us to go into the other order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kay, any problems about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. We had changed our arrangements, but we are able to go back to how we'd originally planned it. So we're happy with it reverting to the original order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you've heard the story. I don't know whether you got the message that they were thinking of calling C-007 first. Are you ready if in fact we start with Mr. Van Baal?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Van Baal, according to the list I received, was due to testify today. This is the first I hear of C-007. But otherwise, I agree. There's something else that I should like to raise, Mr. May. Last night --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Sorry. Let me just get that straight. So we will -- we will finish the witness we're hearing. We will then go on with Mr. Van Baal, but there is one other matter first. I'll return to what you wanted to raise. But the other matter was Witness B-1610. Did you want to ask him any further questions?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is the witness for whom you provided additional transcript yesterday; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, the additional matter yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have nothing to ask in connection with that additional material except to say that it is visible from that material too that earlier he indicated an officer of whom he said was on the spot. He said that he was a representative of the army of Republika Srpska and not of the JNA. So that's what he said in that additional material as well, but I have no reason to call him to ask him more about that. I just wished to draw your attention to that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just one moment. We note what you say, and you can draw our attention to it at an appropriate time. Mr. Nice, it would appear that witness can be released.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The other very short matter is this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There was another matter from Mr. Milosevic. Yes. There was something else you wanted to raise.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to say, Mr. May, that I never received any response regarding my objection to an enormous amount of material that is being disclosed to me. Most recently, there was additional material. In fact, last night I received this pile of material relating to Mr. Van Baal, and this morning, just before entering the courtroom, I received some additional matter relating to Mr. Van Baal who is going to testify now. The night before last, I received this large pile of documents in the Detention Unit regarding Mr. Ramic, who is testifying now. So I received it on the eve of his appearance, and I feel that this is not permissible practice. Furthermore, I should like to remind you once again that many months ago and several times since, I asked you when you think I will have time to review thousands of tapes and about half a million pages that I have been served with, and your response has always been that you will consider the matter. I never received your answer. And this additional provision of piles and piles of documents during the testimony of witnesses I think is totally unacceptable, as is the practice of accumulation of material which it is physically impossible to read through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: During the course of the trial there have been many breaks which has given you the opportunity to review other matter, but of course if there is a specific matter, we will look at it, and in particular, we will inquire of the Prosecution what is going on at the moment. Mr. Nice, can you help us? And it's not satisfactory if a great deal of material is disclosed late. I bear in mind, of course, that you will say that all this material has been disclosed before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Not necessarily on this occasion. I think that so far as Mr. Ramic is concerned, some of the material disclosed under Rule 68 was disclosed late. I'll find out further why it wasn't disclosed earlier. I'll check on the position in relation to General Van Baal before he comes to give evidence, and I'll give you an account then, if I may. But as to Mr. Ramic, there was, I think, some late disclosure as to the various court records, some of which the accused may have turned to or may be turning to this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, what is the full extent, in quantitative terms, of the late disclosure?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In relation to Mr. Ramic, again I'd have to find out. I can't give it to you immediately. But on this occasion I don't think I'm in a position to say it's repeat disclosure. As you will know, the Rule 68 obligations on us are very extensive, which is why, of course, we had another meeting yesterday with the amicus in order to ensure that everything that was being done that could be done, meetings which, as you know, unfortunately the accused's associates do not attend despite always being invited. We endeavour through those meetings to ensure that parameters are set to ensure timely production of Rule 68 material. Whether there has been an oversight on this occasion or a change of parameter or some other reason for the late disclosure, I don't know, but I will look into it and report back to you both as to quantity and the reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we must set aside some time in the next week to consider these matters, but I think now we should get on with the witness. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, this is the amount I received for Mr. Ramic, this pile for Ramic the night before last, for a witness who started testifying yesterday. Secondly, you gave me an additional 45 minutes for Mr. Ramic yesterday, but I have too many documents and more questions, so that 45 minutes will not be sufficient, so I wanted to ask you for an extension of time for the cross-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us begin the cross-examination. We will consider the matter in due course. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One other very short matter. The Chamber will recall that the witness Lilic produced some documents of Council for Harmonisation meetings which contained stenographic notes of what the participants, including the accused, said. They've been submitted for translation. They're now back in draft translation form, about 700 pages in English. The revised authorised translation will probably take several more weeks. There's nothing we can do about that. The accused, of course, has the originals so he will understand the documents should he need to cross-examine on them. I inquire whether the Chamber would like to have these documents, which are potentially valuable documents and may contain exculpatory material on which the accused may rely, or apparently exculpatory material on which he may rely earlier or whether they'd rather wait until several weeks pass and the official versions are available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll have the draft translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have the --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just say, Mr. May, that I don't have those documents of the Council for Harmonisation that Mr. Nice and Mr. Lilic have provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Nice, perhaps you would check that out, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let's have the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: While the witness is coming in, the accused may wish to check Exhibit 469, tabs 39 to 46, I'm informed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, I'm sorry you've been kept waiting. We've had some administrative matters and procedural matters to deal with. When we finished yesterday, I said that you should have the opportunity of seeing Exhibit D184. If that could be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is there any comment, Mr. Ramic, you want to make about that or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have never seen this document before. I see it for the first time now. So it is a terrorist act that was mentioned yesterday with respect to the alleged mining, as Mr. Milosevic said, or blowing up of a train that was heading for Serbia carrying weapons from Brcko. First of all, it is possible that this is an authentic document as it bears the date from 1991. Secondly, what I do notice here, all the signatories of this document are people who later on during the war were actually tormentors and criminals in relation to detained citizens in the town of Brcko. This applies to the signatories of these documents. Those are the very same people. Thirdly, I repeat no weapons were ever taken from Brcko towards Serbia, only in the opposite direction did weapons come. So I also wish to add why would anyone who wanted to protect himself destroy weapons that were being taken away from their environment? They would only welcome such an event. And in the final analysis, even if any such activities were engaged in, I was not aware of them, and quite clearly I do not recollect any response from the army either. The commander of the garrison, Mr. Milinkovic or anyone else did not comment on this, because if they had, I would have remembered it. So if there were any such terrorist preparations, then they may have been engaged in by individuals. That's my comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Wait a moment. The names of the signatories who you say were criminals and tormentors, can you tell us who it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says here the first document noted by Petar Kaurinovic. He was one of the tormentors and investigators during the war in the premises of the then SUP. That is the police premises on the aggressor side. Then there is Zoran Kondic who was also a member of that same group, then Krsto Mihajlovic, also an investigator who was a member of that group, then Zoran Kondic is repeated, and Krsto Mihajlovic. His name appears again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the contents of the statement has nothing to do with this generalised accusations against persons who signed the statement. Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In those days, they were official officers in the Secretariat of the Interior in Brcko. Isn't that right, Mr. Ramic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are persons who were part of the police, and the investigators on the part of the aggressor side after the war. They were indeed policemen before the war as well, but they were operating even after the aggression and the occupation of Brcko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, this statement is from 1991, and it relates to an act of terrorism with respect to which an investigation is undertaken. And this explanation of yours about certain subsequent roles of those people has nothing to do with this statement. My questions relate to that statement.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I did not see these documents, but they were signed only by the persons that I have already described. Therefore, I first wish to state that they may have been compiled retroactively. However, even if they were compiled contemporaneously, their purpose was to provoke dissent on an ethnic basis and discord on an ethnic basis. That is my explanation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the confiscation of explosives and the investigation conducted were designed to provoke ethnic conflict.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday that there was a lot of arms trafficking. I'm not denying that. I am not also denying that some explosives may have been confiscated. I'm just denying the allegation that this was intended to blow up an army convoy heading towards Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But that is what the statement says, the statement that has been shown to you.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that statement was written by these people that I have described.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The statement was given by the man caught with the explosives. Are you also familiar with the fact referred to in that statement that these men mentioned, Vinko Vucicevic, Zeljko Gasparevic, Marko Kovacic, Antun Terzic were all members of the MUP of Croatia and of a special purpose unit, and that, following orders of their commander Martin Matkovic, they were about to carry out this act of sabotage, that is, blowing up a convoy at the railway station in Brcko, carrying military equipment. You have the statements of Ivanovic, Vucicevic, and Gasparevic. Are you denying that too?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not denying that either. That may be true. I'm just repeating that I did not see this document before, and I repeat that in those days I do not recollect this situation as having occurred.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Ramic. Now, tell me, is it true that the bridges across the Sava at Brcko were secured on one side of the river by members of the Brcko police station, which was under your control, and on the other side of the river by members of the MUP of Croatia? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why, then, are you claiming that those bridges were destroyed by the Serbs on the 1st of May?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is quite clear, and it has been proven repeatedly up to now. First of all, we have living witnesses who were there on the spot. Secondly, a series of indications point to the army having done it on the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Brcko side. As I repeat, we have witnesses living today who were guards, policemen on the bridge and who were captured. Each and every one of them claim first that a military vehicle arrived carrying members wearing camouflage army uniforms, that they first captured a group under the bridge and that, after that, a second group arrived which captured a police patrol on the bridge, and a third group brought a vehicle in SMB colour, pushed it onto the bridge, and the captives heard the people talking who were using the Ekavian Serbian dialect, and it is deduced from that that this was a group of elite troops that had come from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So though nothing has been proven, you drew your conclusion. But what has been proven is this act of sabotage by these people who are named in that statement, and you nevertheless conclude that the bridges were destroyed by the Serbs or, rather, the JNA, according to what you are saying now.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so. It was destroyed by the JNA or organised by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you say you have proof of that.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you about the evidence. I didn't know you would ask me about this, and I could provide evidence. There are witnesses who are still alive who were policemen and guards who claim that they were taken captive by men wearing camouflage army uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You've explained that. You don't need to repeat it. So you have on the one hand a statement about an act of sabotage naming all the perpetrators, and on the other hand your allegation that certain unidentified --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. No, Mr. Milosevic. This wastes time. This is argument. You're going to try and argue with the witness. That's not what he's here to do.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let me go on then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, as president of the municipality of Brcko, you certainly know where the Dizdarusa local commune is. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that it was precisely with your approval and the approval of your brother that in the area of Dizdarusa, as far as back as 1991, an armed unit was established which was the 3rd Company of the 108th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to give a document to you which was seized awhile ago, and it shows in the area of Dizdarusa 284 soldiers. This is the document. It has a certification on the last page, like the other documents, stating that it is faithful to the original. Dizdarusa, persons from 1 through 284. There are all kinds of troops there, including crews for anti-aircraft guns and so on and so forth. So the list goes from number 1 to 284. And the date of arrival is the 1st of May, the 1st of May, the 1st of May, and so on and so forth, including all the dates of arrival. The numbers are there of automatic rifles that they were issued with. Please take a look. Take a look at this list.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would also like to have it exhibited, because that is the 108th Brigade, the 3rd Company, Dizdarusa, a list of persons, starting from number 1 all the way up to 284. Please take a look.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I can make a few observations about the exhibits that the accused has produced. They are not documents the Prosecution has seen before, and I the opportunity overnight of trying to find if we have them in our database. We don't. I understand the policy has been generally in the past that such documents are tendered for identification as opposed to exhibited, and I'd ask that be the position in relation to these documents. Most certainly the ones which are numbered 3 thus far. I think it was D179, D180, and D184 about which this witness has expressed reservations as to their authenticity. Certainly he said in respect of D179 and 180, which were the documents dated 1995, that he thought they were fabricated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Plainly the accused is getting a great deal of information, and it may be a matter of course for us to consider when we are considering how much support he has. Where would such documents have come from do you think, Ms. Pack?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I would have thought they would come from the authorities in Republika Srpska, because it seems to me that they are -- they are -- well, they're headed Republika Srpska, Brcko Public Security Station. I think they have an authentication case stamp, at least on some of them on the reverse. I'm afraid I don't understand it because it's in Cyrillic. Perhaps the accused might be able to assist as to what that says. I should imagine that that's where they're from. I only say -- I don't push this but I say just generally it may be this would give the opportunity to the Prosecution to examine these documents further and ascertain their authenticity if they're marked for identification rather than exhibited now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. The answer, Ms. Pack, is this, that we will not change the position about these documents, but if it proves in due course that they are not authentic and you've got evidence to challenge them, of course you can bring that forward. And if it proves to be unauthentic, they won't be taken any notice of. And furthermore, it will tell us something about the source from which they've come. On the other hand, if they're authentic, we'll have to consider what weight to give them. The fact that documents are admitted does not mean to say they are accepted as truthful or their content is truthful. Yes, Mr. Ramic. I'm sorry. You've been looking at that document. Is there anything you want to say about that one? This is the list, apparently, as alleged -- just a moment. Let me get this right. Is this right: It's alleged to be a list of a company formed in 1991 with 284 members, or a brigade. Is that what it claims to be? Could you tell us that and then you can comment on it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have quite a few things to say in relation to this document. First of all, on the front page of this document it says that it is the 108th Brigade, the 3rd Company, in Dizdarusa. I would like to clarify the fact that the 108th Brigade was established on the 17th of May, 1992. And the war and the occupation of Brcko took place on the 1st of May. That is to say 17 days after the occupation while the aggressor side had already committed an aggression vis-a-vis the territory of Brcko that had remained free. This list actually constitutes a list of the entire male population of the local commune of Dizdarusa. It was obviously compiled with the intention of probably collecting some men on the basis of this list. But I repeat, this could have taken place only after the 17th of May, 1992, because until then, the name, the 108th Brigade, did not exist at all. Another thing, this document is stamped by Republika Srpska. It bears a seal of Republika Srpska; that is to say, that it was found and authenticated probably later. This also indicates that its validity is in line with such a view, and that's probably clear. On the basis of that, I conclude that this is no document indicating the existence of some kind of 3rd Company of some 108th Brigade before the war actually started. That's my comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, please take a look at this starting from number 1. You can see that there is a date when each and every soldier or member joined in, and that was the 1st of May, and then in order. There are many of them who joined up on the 1st of May because that's when the war broke out over there. Secondly, is it correct that when you refer to the stamp of Republika Srpska, that you are actually referring to the authentication of the document itself, because that's what it says on the reverse side of each and every document, that this was done in order to authenticate the fact that this is a photocopy which is fully identical to the original. So this is practically a form, and it is accompanied by this seal, and it says "Is equal to the original and consists of ten pages." So this is the official authentication of documents that were found. The 3rd Company --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you know making speeches is not allowed. You can ask the witness questions. Now, what the accused seems to be putting, Mr. Ramic, is that this is a genuine document which has been found by the Republika Srpska, and that is stamped on it, and he seems to be suggesting that it's an earlier date than the 17th of May, 1992, which you suggest. Can you help as to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I've been trying to say the following: This document is a list of men from the local commune of Dizdarusa. By no means does it constitute a list of some kind of a company. It is not signed by any designated official from the command of the brigade or the command of the company. Absolutely there is no proper list here, which means that it could have been written by anybody. Secondly, Your Honours, I've been trying to say that even if we were to accept that this is something authentic by way of a list, it can by no means mean that this was done before the 108th Brigade was established. And I repeat, the 108th Brigade, that is a well known thing, was established on the 17th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, please read the date when people joined up, starting from number 1. Doesn't it say the 1st of May?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, what you call this date of joining up is not what is written here. It says the date of arrival. That's what's written here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, date of arrival in the unit.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it doesn't say the date of arrival in the unit. It says date of arrival. It doesn't mean that it has to be a unit necessarily.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does it say the 1st of May?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says the 1st of May, et cetera, et cetera, it's not only the 1st of May, so on and so forth. However, I claim that no company could have been established on the 1st of May, because the 108th Brigade did not exist, and I believe that this is quite clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This could have been proclaimed to be part of the 108th Brigade a few days later, but it could have changed names, but it's the 3rd Company of Dizdarusa.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the occupation of Brcko took place on the 1st of May. Even if I were to accept what you are claiming now, this could have happened only after the moment of occupation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. All right, Mr. Ramic. I'm going to show something else to you now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No you're not. We're going to look at that document first of all.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please give it to the amici. One speaks Serbian, and he can read it and he can tell you what kind of a document this is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we will do the following: We will -- we will look at it ourselves, so we'll ask the usher to go and get the document and hand it to the Bench. We'll then decide what to do with it next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll mark this one for identification since there is a dispute about its nature.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just -- go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: D. We'll give it now to the Prosecution to look at briefly and then hand it to the amicus. In due course, if need be, the Prosecution can have it back. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Mr. Ramic, I'm sorry. You were going to say something. Yes. What do you want to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I wanted to say that this is a list of men from the local commune, and somebody wrote this date in hand, the 1st of May, and it just meant that these men lived in the territory of that local commune on that date, nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So the fact that it is written that this is the 3rd Company from Dizdarusa, that doesn't mean that it's a military formation? That it's a list of civilians who lived at that locality; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean that that is what it means.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. If that's what it means, then here's another document that has to do with this same company. It is also handwritten. It is also an original. It also has a certification coming from the appropriate authority that it is identical to the original, and then there is the company number and then the 1st Platoon, and then its entire composition, and then the 2nd Platoon, and then various squads, the 1st, 2nd, 3rd Platoons, then it can be seen who is anti-armour, who is a guide, who is in reconnaissance. So it is all there. And as you can see, this is a formation of the Muslim army. Please take a look at this document as well. It can be seen that you have platoons, that you have a squad for recoilless guns, a squad for anti-aircraft guns, and a squad for mortars. So this is the Dizdarusa, the 3rd Company. Please take a look at this document and you will realise that this is a military formation, if the first document was not sufficient because it only said the 3rd Company. You will see all the platoons and squads here as well. Mr. Ramic, while you're looking at this, is it correct that Dedovic Ramiz was commander of the 1st Platoon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just one moment. Let the witness first of all have a look and then you can ask him some questions about it when he's had the opportunity to comment. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I've been looking through this document, and for me it constitutes a list that includes the commands of platoons, et cetera, et cetera, and it is entitled, "The 108th Brigade, Dizdarusa, the 3rd Company." There is no original date here which could show when this was compiled. So this may be a list of some kind of composition but by no means could it have been compiled prior to the 17th of May. Another thing: Mr. Milosevic, this was not a Muslim army. If that's the army we're talking about, it was the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And as proof of the fact that it was a multi-ethnic army, please take a look at this list that you're giving me. The 5th Platoon, the commander of the 5th Platoon is Dragan Hajduk. A person with that kind of name certainly was not a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But look at the names. 95 per cent of them are Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. The local commune of Dizdarusa had a population which was 95 per cent Muslim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, is the list handwritten or typed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is a handwritten list. It is not typed, and I repeat, I do not see any reliable or competent person as a signatory of the list or anybody who had any command function in the 108th Brigade. There is no signature. So it is a list written by hand which, again, could have been written by anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, are you claiming that those were not the people who constituted a military unit that was known as the 3rd Company and their division into platoons? The 1st commander Ramiz Dedovic, the 2nd Amir Serifovic, Ramiz Halilovic of the 3rd Platoon, Hazim Hasanovic of the 4th Platoon, and Dragan Hajduk of the 5th Platoon that you mentioned a moment ago. Isn't all that written on this list? Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I'm not denying this. Maybe you didn't understand what I was saying. I am saying that this list, we can't tell when it was compiled. That is not clear. Secondly, if it was compiled and if it is original, it could only have been compiled after the 17th of May. Thirdly, I am not denying that there was a Dizdarusa company in the 108th Brigade, but it came into being after the 17th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll have a look at this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps you could assist, Mr. Ramic. This is a handwritten document. We can't read, of course, the writing on it, but it appears to be a list, as I understand your evidence, of the 3rd Company, 108th Brigade. It's handwritten. It's in -- appears to be in some sort of formation. But it's your evidence that there was such a company of such a brigade but that it was formed after the occupation; is that right? So really, there's no --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, precisely so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So there is a dispute that there was such an organisation. The only issue which is apparently in dispute is when it was formed. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll admit this. Give it the next number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If I could hand it in. Thank you. Yes. Let everybody see it, please. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, the first document I showed you about the 3rd Company Dizdarusa contains the date of the 1st of May that you yourself have read out?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have been over that. We're not going back to it. Again, it's a case of your arguing with the witness. You've heard his evidence. There is no point going over it again. We will have to make a decision about this in due course.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it clear that on that list next to the names of persons there's an indication of the type and serial number of the weapon issued to that person? Have you managed to look at that when you looked at the document? I'm talking about the first list. From Dizdarusa.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There are certain numbers and indications, markings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doesn't AP mean an automatic rifle and next to it the serial number consisting of several digits?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what it means. I'm not denying that it could not be interpreted that way. It could be something else also. But I am repeating once again the company could have existed only after the 17th of May and, therefore, also the armaments of that weapon -- of that company. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I think that we will now have a clearer indication regarding the time. I'm asking you, Mr. Ramic, is it true that as early as 1991, as in Dizdarusa, you formed a similar unit in a local commune called Stari Rasadnik and that there was a so-called spatial unit and a manoeuvering unit consisting of companies and platoons? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's not right. Very well, then. I'll give you now a document. Local commune it says up there, Stari Rasadnik, manoeuvre unit, manoeuvreing unit which means a mobile unit. This is a typed document this time, and it is signed by the Staff Commander of the Territorial Defence of the local commune Meksud Imamovic. You know Meksud Imamovic, I assume?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't quite remember, but I'm not denying that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, he signed this document, and in handwriting he wrote on each page: "Place of mobilisation will be secret, but in the case of an emergency, the -- where the unit will rally will be indicated on the call-up paper." Which means that the unit was formed before, because if it was formed after the war broke out, why would the place of reporting be secret? And on each page it is indicated that the place -- rallying place will be secret, but in case of urgency, the place will be indicated on the call-up paper. And at the end, it says the commander of the TO staff, Meksud Imamovic. You have here mortar crews of 82-millimetre mortars, trucks. The specialties are indicated of individual members of the unit. As far as I can see, again all of them are Muslims. So we're talking about the Stari Rasadnik local commune, a manoeuvre, a mobile unit, and an indication that the place of mobilisation will be kept secret but should an urgent need arise, it will be indicated on the call-up paper. And you have the signature of Meksud Imamovic whom you don't see to remember; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may know him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, I see. You may know him. Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness see the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Here, I've opened it on the page with his signature, and then you can look at it from the very beginning, from page 1.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to comment on this document as follows: Again, this is a list of men from a local commune who formed squads of Territorial Defence, but it is not clear when this document was compiled. That is the first point. Secondly, Mr. Milosevic, mention is made here of the Territorial Defence of the local commune. Your Honours, I wish to state that after the events of the 1st of May and after the already-mentioned appearance on local television and disclosure by television that the war had started, that is the attack by the aggressor JNA of the local commune of Dizdarusa - in fact, this was in the afternoon, about 4.00 p.m. - after that I only just managed to get out of that area. And that same day, in the evening after this, being the president of the municipality, I gave instructions for the Territorial Defence to be formed on the free part of the territory. So if that is the list of that Territorial Defence, I am not denying it, but I repeat that the date is lacking on this document, and we can discuss that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But look, on page 1, 2, and 3, in the right-hand margin there is this note written every time by Meksud Imamovic, saying that the place of mobilisation will be kept secret, but in the case of an urgent need or an emergency, it will be indicated on the call-up paper.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, reference is made of the place of mobilisation. I wish to remind you that the word "mobilisation" means rallying and gathering for the purpose of forming a military unit, which means that it had still not been formed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Surely the existing military unit that had been formed, this note relates to that unit, that it is then that it will be mobilised, so that a unit is ready. And you can see from the companies and squads that the unit is ready. And it says that the place of mobilisation shall be kept secret, but in the case of an emergency, it will be indicated on the call-up paper.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is in dispute, Mr. Milosevic? I'm not denying that Territorial Defence units were formed in local communities defending themselves from the aggression after the aggression took place about 4.00 p.m. on the 1st of May. I'm not denying that. After that, Territorial Defence units were formed. So after the aggression, a Territorial Defence was being formed in free territorial -- free local communes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then the place of mobilisation was kept secret, and the Territorial Defence did not operate; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to stop this. I'm going to stop this. You've had your opportunity to cross-examine about this document, and you're now arguing with the witness again. Give it the next number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Inaudible]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, if we can have it back, please, the document. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, I assume you're familiar with the local commune Brod.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have complete data about the Brod local commune, the special unit commanded by Pasic Ismet, and then the manoeuvre unit, or the mobile unit, divided up into squads, companies, the couriers. This is quite a voluminous document speaking of a very numerically large military formation for this local commune alone, that is, the Brod local commune. They even have a part of the military police. And at the end, it says that the place of mobilisation will be Johak, across the river. That is what is indicated at the end of this document consisting of several pages. And again there is a certification indicating that it is true to the original, the certification being made by the authorities of Republika Srpska as these documents are that they confiscated during the war. So please look at this document. It is typewritten, and it relates to the local commune of Brod.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Would you like to look at it, Mr. Ramic. It doesn't seem to have got a date, as far as I can see. If it has one, please tell us. If your comments are the same, perhaps you can just say that and we could get on more quickly, if we're going to have a number of these documents.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is a similar document that Mr. Milosevic is producing here, a list of men from the local commune formed into platoons and similar units of the Territorial Defence of that local commune. It does not have a date. What I am claiming is that this is a list -- if it is original, because there is no proof that it is original. It is typewritten and certified with a stamp of Republika Srpska, which means retroactively. There's no signature nor any name of a person who could be considered responsible, a commander. But if it is original, I repeat it could only have come into being after my instructions to form Territorial Defence units in free local communes. And this occurred after the occupation of the town of Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, you were president of the municipality. I assume you know well that there is a secretariat for administration in the municipality where documents are certified and stamped to indicate that a document or a photocopy of the document is true to the original. So that is what you will see on the back of each page, a stamp of the competent body in the municipality, indicating that the photocopy is identical with the original. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I am not denying the method of certification of documents that you have told us about, but I am saying that this is a stamp of Republika Srpska dated 1994. So that is absolutely retroactive, many years later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Surely when the documents were confiscated, after the confiscation who knows how much later they made copies and certified that the copies were true to the original.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, are you denying the following: That in 1994 Republika Srpska could have, over a period of several years, learnt all the names of the combatants of the 108th Brigade? Furthermore, all the documents of citizens stayed behind in the archives, so can you deny that this was not a document construed in 1994 by the authorities of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will make a decision about this document. It's no point arguing about it. We'll give it the next number, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, might I again make the observation that this document be admitted marked for ID on the basis of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us see it. It's not disputed that there was a territorial unit. It's not disputed that this may have been a list, although it's not plain, when it came into being. The document is stamped, as is accepted. It is a list for what it's worth. The crucial issue is when it came into existence, and as to that there is no evidence on the document. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. So we will admit it. If you, in due course, can cause doubt on its authenticity, then that will mean it's not taken any notice of, but for these purposes we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, tell me, please, these local communes - Brod, Dizdarusa, Stari Rasadnik - in the territory that you held during the war or was this territory held by the Serb forces? Is this the territory that was held by you throughout the war; Dizdarusa, Brod, Stari Rasadnik?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the moment of occupation, that is to say the 1st of May, 1992, this was territory that was free territory, territory where we were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And for how long did this territory remain free, as you had put it, in your opinion? When did this territory stop being free territory according to your information?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the war, there were war operations, and the aggressor side pushed us out of these territories. I cannot say anything for sure now, but we did keep parts of the city of Brcko free.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you about these three local communes that I referred to just now. How long were they in the hands of your forces? Just tell me that.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were free during -- well, local commune of Dizdarusa and the local commune of Rasadnik and the local commune of Brod were free for a few months, perhaps even for a year from when the war broke out, that is to say, from the 1st of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So these formations were held -- so these units held this territory?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These territories were protected and held by the units of the 108th Brigade, and I'm not denying that within these units there weren't any platoons or squads from these units -- from these local communes. They were integral parts of the 108th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us just wait for them to put their headphones on again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we will give you until the end of this session, which means you will have had rather more than 20 minutes more than you've already told, i.e., a 50 per cent extension, which will be more than enough. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then I will just try to include these documents, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who Sakovic Semso is?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he president of the local commune of Brodusa and director of the Sava company?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he involved in activities related to the procurement of weapons for Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And is it correct that in the local commune of Stari Rasadnik, Meksud Imamovic, Becirevic Nedzad, Nejdelko Esad, Asic Ahmed [phoen], Sukalac Mujo [phoen], Mustafa Halilovic, and Ismail Semsudin were in charge of receiving these weapons in this local commune? Is that correct or is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, in order to be able to answer your question, I have no idea what kind of weapons you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Since you have no idea what kind of weapons I'm talking about -- there weren't any weapons there, is that what you're trying to say? So all the weapons listed in these documents were invented?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no weapons in an organised and systematic fashion until the aggression took place on the 1st of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. What I have here is information similar to the kind I showed yesterday, and it says here: "In Brcko, Brka, Maoca, the road and settlements there were only secured by armed Muslims. Later on it became obvious that they wanted to have such persons on patrols so that weapons could be transported. The director of KRO Sava was Semso."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: This is too fast for the interpreters. The interpreters note it is being read too fast and the interpreters don't have these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Don't read too quickly, Mr. Milosevic. Just remember the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May, but my time is short. Of course I'll bear that in mind too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then it says: "The arming of members of the SDS was done through the Ramic brothers, the top people -" that's you and your brother - "Semso Isakovic; and the director of the work organisation Laser, Vejzovic Ibrahim; director of the customs zone, Didais Ismet [phoen]; the director of the work organisation Zitopromet, Drpljanin Saban. And weapons for the most part came from Croatia through the old bridge on the Sava River. Operations related to arms deliveries were carried out by Pezerovic Zekerija and Hasim. He held a weapons shop legally, and then with the assistance of a policeman on the bridge --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, look. You're taking up your time reading this entire document out. Just try and summarise it and put it to the witness. What is the point of this? What is the point of all this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is what I read out correct, Mr. Ramic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it correct that people of Serb ethnicity, for example, Ilic Zivko who had a shop with mixed goods in Gornji Rahic, and a year before the war he had to leave his shop and also the house that he had in Stari Rasadnik, he did not sleep there for five or six months before the war broke out, precisely because of such developments. Was this characteristic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I just make a brief comment? Mr. Milosevic, you yourself collide with what you've been saying. Yesterday you were trying to prove to me that the police, and this police were all ethnic Bosniaks, stopped the smuggling of weapons. Now you're telling me today that this same police made it possible to carry out armament, and you say that I was one of the persons who organised this. That's the first thing I wish to say. Please do not interrupt me, because I have not finished, Mr. Milosevic. Yesterday you said to me that there was some kind of a meeting in Rasadnik concerning the organisation of Stragar [phoen] or whatever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We haven't got time.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have got time. I have to answer you. And you mention the name of a person who is an ethnic Serb and now you're telling me that these persons of Serb ethnicity had to flee from Stari Rasadnik. Are you not contradicting yourself?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am quoting an Official Note to you, Mr. Ramic, and this was written in Brcko and it describes all your activities before the war and I would just like to have it exhibited here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness see the document so he can comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I've highlighted what I believe are the most important parts in order to save time. Do you know these persons? Did they do what is written there or not?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know -- well, this is a long list of people. I know quite a few of them. Semso Isakovic, you mentioned him and I know him well. And also these other people you mentioned, I know them well too. I deny that they organised and carried out any type of armament before the 1st of May, 1992. So that's what I'm denying. Secondly, this document that you call a document also bears the date of the 18th of October, 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, like the previous ones that contain documents about what was going on there then.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. So this means that this document was compiled at the very end of the war, and I think that the war was almost over or over at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, then, is it correct that some weapons were used, and I claim that you procured them in this way, were used to open fire against the JNA in the JNA garrison?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You say on page 8 of your statement that as for the rest of the war, in Brcko, May 1992, that you spent that in the free part of Brcko. That is your very own expression.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that is what I wrote. It means the free part of the municipality of Brcko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So these local communes that you've described and that we've been discussing did not belong to that part?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did. They did too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Until when?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we just mentioned that awhile ago. Rasadnik and Dizdarusa were free for a few months. I cannot tell you exactly for how long.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me -- but since they were free, tell me, what did you use to defend those areas that you called free areas if you did not have any weapons?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, that is quite clear. In the Yugoslavia that disappeared, a certain number of people had their very own weapons, hunting weapons or something similar to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But --

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, let me answer. A number of people were members of the legal pre-war organisation of the Territorial Defence, so they had weapons. A number of people were professionals in the police force or in the reserve police force. They also had weapons. So those are the weapons concerned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Ramic. I really haven't got the time to go into that any further now, but it is quite clear that you had to have weapons if you managed, as you had put it, to hold a certain part of Brcko so that it would not be taken. Do you know that as far as you are concerned and your brother and another person and other persons in Republika Srpska, on the 9th of November, 1995, criminal charges were brought against you indicting you of the crime of armed rebellion? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that. I had heard about this only accidentally after the war was over, and I think that it was towards the end of 1995 or beginning of 1996 that we were accused of some kind of a war crime. It is only then that I heard about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you know -- I am going to let the witness have a look at these documents all together, because these are court documents, that the public prosecutor's office on the 9th of June, 1994, indicted you for the crime of a war crime against the civilian population. Are you aware of that? And you're the first indictee listed in that indictment. So this is the 9th of June, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the document that you refer to. That is something that I heard about only after the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you denying that you issued an order for the attack against the Serb village of Bukovac that was carried out in September 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I deny that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, you deny it. And that then you killed a great many Serbs and you took the rest to concentration camps where they were tortured, abused and some were even physically liquidated. All of this is written in this indictment.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, that is what is written in a document which, as you said yourself, was compiled in 1994 concerning events from 1992. Your Honours, may I just make a comment? Your Honours, I wish to make a comment. The mentioned indictment against me and against some other persons at the end of the war is something that was construed. It is a construction that was characteristic of the aggressor side; after having committed crimes, they accuse the victim of such things. That is the first point I wish to make. Secondly, Mr. Milosevic, not even theoretically let alone practically I could not have issued an order for an attack against this village that you have just referred to for a simple reason; because already at that time the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was already in existence, it had its own chain of command, and I as a representative of the civilian authorities was outside that chain of command, so this was not possible even theoretically.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you did not order an attack against the civilian population and these civilians that are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He said that. The witness has dealt with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these civilians that are mentioned in this indictment, were they killed or not? Were they taken to concentration camps or not? Were they tortured or not? Just answer that.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, that is a farce, what you've just referred to, and you know that. Your Honours, please bear in mind that this is a matter of accusing the victim, not the criminal, and that was characteristic of the Serb side and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, we have these matters in mind. We've heard this sort of allegation against witnesses before, and you must understand that if we admit these documents, we do so merely as documents and it doesn't mean that we put any weight on them at all. We will have to consider them in the light of all the evidence. We know that allegations were made against victims because we've heard that they've been made. So it's a matter that we have in mind. Yes. Let us tidy up the documents. The document of the 18th of October -- just a moment -- the 18th of October will be admitted for -- marked for identification. I have it here. I'll hand it in. We'll get the next number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D189, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Do you want to -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Further on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you want to exhibit this indictment, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I've already quoted three documents, Mr. May, because I'm saving time. And I have because I'm saving time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that there was an indictment issued against you for the attacks on Vujicici, Gajevi, and Bukovac Serb villages, and this has to do with several persons, in September 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to make a comment in this regard as well. Mr. Milosevic, you're talking about the same thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are talking about the Bukvik case. Mr. Milosevic, I know this better than you know. I know that next to Bukvik is the village of Bukovac, the village of Vitanovici, and the hamlets that you mentioned. All of this is within the area within this territory. Your Honours, in September 1992, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina - rather the 108th Brigade - had a clash with the aggressor side at those positions, and the result of these -- this conflict are probably some casualties that Mr. Milosevic referred to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those people who were taken to concentration camps and where their skulls were broken and where they were beaten -- cut up and beaten up, is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Absolutely not. You've already put these kind of allegations. The witness has denied them. They're not improved by repeating them. Now, let's get on. You've got two minutes left.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, these are different indictments pertaining to different villages, although Mr. Ramic says that it is all one and the same thing. So please bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that the court in Brcko issued on the 5th of July, 1995, a sentence in which you were convicted of various crimes, and you and your brother Ibrahim, and it was a 15-year prison sentence?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are talking about the document that I mentioned I had heard about in 1995. That is what I heard about, that it was some kind of a court that had convicted me of some kind of war crimes. This is a pure farce. And this means playing games with the crimes of one side, and they want to ascribe it to another side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please. This is a judgement of a court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, he's dealt with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's dealt with it. He says it was a farce. Now, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that this is a farce, Mr. May. And all of these are facts. These are court documents, and this is a judgement. This is no longer an indictment. This is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Your time is now up. You've made the point. We will consider what to do with all the court documents together, and after the -- after the adjournment we will hear from the amicus, if he has any questions, and then the Prosecution. We will adjourn now. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked for these court documents to be admitted into evidence. I assume that Mr. Ramic is not going to challenge their authenticity.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you seeking my answer for this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. No. We know what your answer to this is. We'll consider what to do about them and then we will adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will admit the court documents. We do so without, of course, passing any judgement upon them or also indicating whether they have any weight at all. We do so merely to record the fact that such documents are in existence. We will begin with the indictments. Have you got those documents, Mr. Milosevic? Perhaps you could hand the two indictments in, and we'll deal with the judgement separately.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here they are, Mr. May. I have the indictment dated the 9th of November, 1995, or, rather, criminal charges, then the indictment of the 9th of June, 1994. I have quoted from all of them. Then the indictment of the 14th of July, 1994; the indictment of the 16th of July, 1994; the indictment of the 26th of July, 1994; and judgement -- the judgement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's -- just a moment. Let's have the indictments first, all together, and we'll just give them one number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. That's the indictments. And the judgement we will give the next number to. If you would hand that in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We will get the number for the judgement, please. 191. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, were you aware of these indictments and the charges?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't know about them. I learnt quite by coincidence after this date when those alleged indictments were issued. So I think this was -- I'm not quite sure whether it was November or December, 1995, or January, February, 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So I take it then you were never arrested pursuant to these indictments.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, of course not. That's out of the question. And I consider this to be an absolute farce. I could say a lot of things about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The judgement then would have been done in absentia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Probably. Probably. I had no idea about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Sorry. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, several days ago - or to be precise, on the 8th of September, 2003 - as amici we received quite a large number of documents under Rule 68, containing exculpatory elements, and among them - I don't want to fatigue you with all of them - and in view of what Mr. Slobodan Milosevic has already raised, I have selected only a few documents from 1993. That is prior to the establishment of this Tribunal. Two documents are dated January 1993 and two are from February of the same year. In all four cases, that is, all four documents relate to criminal charges for the crime -- for war crimes against civilian population pursuant to Article 142 of the Criminal Code of the SFRY; and pursuant to all those criminal charges, the event, the place, the date, the victims are indicated. And in all those criminal charges, the first accused is Mustafa Ramic. I have four others, but I don't want to tire you with them. I think that this could be something that you should take into consideration as it comes from the OTP. Questioned by Mr. Tapuskovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would just like to ask the witness whether he is aware of the events covered by these charges, where it is stated that the locals of the village of Bukovac recognised you as having participated in certain acts that you are charged with in these indictments.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may explain. You're asking me to respond regarding events.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, for example, let us take this event of the 11th of February [as interpreted], 1992 at 1730 hours. The names of victims are mentioned. Eight persons were killed, and it says here that certain number of inhabitants of the village of Bukovac recognised you as the perpetrator of those acts. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A moment ago you said the 11th of February, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, the act was committed on the 11th of September, 1992, by units within the 108th Brigade, and then you are mentioned as the first, having been identified by some inhabitants of the village of Bukovac. Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, allow me to expand on this to be able to answer the question. Within the free territory of Brcko where I was amongst others and which was defended by the 108th Brigade, there was an area with the village of Bukvik including the other mentioned villages far behind the frontline about 7 or 10 kilometres behind. And this area is an area of ethnically pure Serb villages, and we knew there was an organised armed group there. However, the BH army did not go into that area, and there were no incidents for all of four months. So the aggression or, rather, the occupation of Brcko occurred on the 1st of May, 1992. Then we have May, June, July, August, and events started happening at the beginning of September. Throughout this period of time, the brigade endeavoured on several occasions to talked to these armed men, members of some sort of military structure in those villages, for them to be peacefully disarmed so that this area too could join in the defence. These talks went on for a long time, and there were no conflicts. However, I wish to point out on several occasions during that period, what happened was that the occupiers broke into areas that it wanted to annex and committed a number of crimes. Prompted by this and also on the basis of reports received after the line of communication was cut between the other side and this group, that is the occupiers' side and these villages, this line of communications went through our free territory, and when it was cut it was established that the occupying side was preparing to enter into that area. I learnt about this all subsequently from the command of the 108th Brigade, because I personally was not involved in this as I was the civilian representative of the authorities. What happened was that a representative of the brigade tried once again with a white flag to enter this village and to talk to the people, and he was killed. After that a conflict broke out and got out of control. I don't know exactly what happened there, but anyway, the 108th Brigade did take control of the area, and I must say that they found large quantities of weapons, four heavy machine-guns, several grenade launchers, about 100 to 200 automatic rifles, lots of explosives, bombs, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any victims on the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe there were. But what I'm trying to say is all those victims were armed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you just say something in connection with the second criminal charges pressed against you. Reference is made to an attack on the village of Bijela in Brcko municipality committed on the 11th of June within 1130 on 1400 hours, and in this attack, according to these criminal charges, you are the first suspect. Again there were a number of victims. Do you know anything about this event?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The village of Bijela is deep within the free territory behind the frontline some 15 or 20 kilometres behind it. You should bear that in mind first of all. Secondly, that village had a mixed population with about 70 per cent of the locals being of Croat ethnicity and 30 of Serb ethnicity. And from the very beginning of the armed conflict, the moment of occupation, the 1st of May, this village joined in the defence together with the other structures. I am not denying that there was an attack on that village, and I cannot deny that something happened that I was not aware of. And a further comment on my part, Your Honours, which I would like you to bear in mind, I'm probably mentioned there as the person who headed the civilian authority at the time. And the mention of my name within the context of the war, conflicts, and battles is absolutely absurd.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I wouldn't like to dwell on those documents any further, but I think that the Court should have them to look at them as these are documents disclosed by the OTP. They are four criminal reports, and I'd like to have them exhibited, I think?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, give them the next C number, court number.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. This first page bears my signature, but that is how I received it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That can have a number in a moment. Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would just like to ask the witness a few things about what the Yugoslav People's Army did when all this started on the 1st of May and it has to do with the events on the bridges. You were questioned in great detail about this event, Witness, on the 10th and 12th of December by the Prosecution. So could the Prosecution give the witness his statement which he gave in December 1998. Mr. Ramic, would you look at page 7, please, fourth paragraph. Here is what you said at the time regarding the events in connection with the blowing up of the bridges. In the fourth paragraph you said: "Three days before the bridges were blown up, I was so concerned about the possibility of conflict that I sent my family to Zagreb." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the next paragraph you say: "By this time I noticed I was being followed." Who was following you?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer to that question also requires some explanation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's not essential, Your Honours. My question really is that you said that, "The night when the bridges were blown up, I spent that night at my sister's." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you had no direct knowledge as to what exactly was going on at the bridges?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand the question. What do you mean I didn't have any knowledge. About what?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
