utterances.text: You said that you were staying at your sister's. Throughout your statement, which you have in front of you, you did not mention anywhere that the JNA had anything to do with the blowing up of the bridges. Nowhere did you say that. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Look at page 8, paragraph 3. When you were making a statement and when you were interviewed by the OTP, and on the day it happened, you said: "Somebody tried to provoke a conflict by blowing up the bridges." Nowhere did you say that the JNA had anything to do with the blowing up of the bridges in your statement of December 1998. Why? Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, I explained a moment ago that the blowing up of the bridges was done by the Yugoslav army, its representatives, and it was organised by it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that, but I'm asking you why you didn't say this in your statement.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are misinterpreting this paragraph. What I am saying, that in the conversations on that day, that is the 30th of May in the morning, the day before the occupation, in the negotiations with the army, it was clear to me and to us who did it and why. I tried to prevent the outbreak of the conflict, and of course the main thing I had to do was to talk to the army, the potential opposite party. And in those negotiations, to achieve what I wanted, that is to calm the situation down rather than provoke the conflict, I couldn't start the talks by accusing them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that, but why didn't you tell the investigators what you said today, that is that the Yugoslav People's Army had blown up the bridges? Why didn't you say that in 1998? I can understand that you didn't say that two days after the event, but why didn't you say it in 1998? Why didn't you tell the OTP that straight away? What is your explanation?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably the conversation did not take that course. Maybe they didn't ask me. Maybe at that point in time I didn't say that. But I didn't say that anyone else had done it or that I didn't know who had done it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you explain what was the interest of the Yugoslav People's Army which had heavy weapons, tanks that were coming to and from Serbia, bringing them there or taking them away from there, what interest would the JNA have to be deprived of bridges? Because a serious army such as the JNA was at the time simply couldn't function without bridges. So how would it be in the interests of the JNA to destroy the bridges when their conflicts had not even started?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is where the answer lies, Mr. Tapuskovic. The interest was because that bridge was the umbilical cord linking Brcko and Croatia, which by then was already winning the war against that army. So that on the other side there was a free territory which could have assisted free Brcko, and the army wanted to cut that off, to cut off our rear. That was -- the second reason was that by destroying the bridges, and it used an excessive amount of explosives intentionally, which caused absolute panic in town so that it was impossible to organise any defence properly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you mentioned that at the time there were about 150 civilians on the bridge when it was blown up. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These were civilians that were crossing the bridge coming from Croatia, citizens returning home who were working somewhere, as gastarbeiters who were returning home for the May Day holidays, women and children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when the bridge was blown up they were all on the bridge?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that there were very many casualties? You never mention that anywhere in your earlier statements. You didn't even mention knowing of any single victim.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, maybe that is not stated in this written document, but there are plenty of -- there's plenty of evidence, witness statements. There were more than 100 casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Pack.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can the witness be handed Defence Exhibits D190 and D191.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: While that's happening we'll get the C number, the court number for the last bundle.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: C13. Re-examined by Ms. Pack:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, look at the first pages of those two documents you've been handed. Just the front page.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before today, have you seen either of those documents that you've been handed before?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw it only yesterday when you showed them to me, madam, but never before that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you seen an indictment before, or a judgement issued by the Republika Srpska authorities?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't ever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You live now in Sarajevo. Have you returned to Brcko since you left?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I go to Brcko very often.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have family in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I do have family there. Two of my brothers live there and my sister lives there and some other members of my family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you or they received ever any documentation about criminal proceedings against you or details of specific charges against you?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards what you've been saying to me now and what you've shown me, no, never. Nobody ever received any such thing. I haven't been informed of any such thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But, Ms. Pack, I couldn't understand him when he said that he had seen the document yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Perhaps I can ask the witness just to look at each document in turn.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first document, D190, look at the first page and look, please, at what it's headed. Is it an indictment?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says, "Criminal report," dated the 9th of November, 1995, by the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see this specific document yesterday or when you arrived in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not yesterday. Your Honours, I made a mistake. When I arrived in The Hague, at one point in time you showed it to me, but it wasn't yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Perhaps the witness can be handed the amicus exhibit, the C number, C13.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, I don't want to confuse you, but this is a third document, and again you can see that that document has a different heading. Perhaps you could identify the date of that document and identify the heading of that document.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a criminal report submitted by the military prosecutor's office in Bijeljina, and it's dated the 18th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it in fact that document and documents of a similar nature to that which were shown to you on your arrival at The Hague?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I don't want to confuse the witness, Your Honour, but the documents produced by the accused today aren't documents held by the OTP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a couple of further questions, Mr. Ramic. Have steps ever been taken to bring you or any of the other individuals named on that document to trial?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. I was not informed, anyway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell the Court, please, the circumstances in which you first heard of any criminal proceedings against you.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already said a short while ago, during our previous discussion, that regarding the judgement pertaining to alleged war crimes in which I'm mentioned too, I heard about that quite accidentally. I cannot say when and where exactly. Somebody told me about this or somebody showed me an excerpt from a newspaper article at the time, and it came from the side of occupied Brcko. But this was already 1995 or 1996. And the headline said, "Accused of war crimes," and then my name is mentioned in the text. It's the first time I ever heard of this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell the Court, please, have you heard since that time of any further matters relating to those charges?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. This was a year and a half ago. I read in the newspapers that the court in Brcko, in the district of Brcko, that's what it is nowadays, so the court in Brcko pardoned the persons accused for war crimes. My name is mentioned too, and I was surprised by this. May I make a further comment? May I speak about this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Briefly, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I was surprised, and I addressed the court in writing. I managed to find their telephone number too, and I phoned this judge and I asked what kind of war crime was involved, and I wrote a letter of protest, asking them to stop all proceedings and not to mention me as a war criminal at all and that I would not accept any kind of pardon or amnesty for something I had never done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ms. Pack, I think we need to get to the bottom of this story, these allegations having been made. If it's right that the Court has issued an amnesty, then it's obviously something this Court should know about because it might have an effect on our understanding of the situation. So perhaps the Prosecution would look into that and come up with an answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes, we'll look into that. The only documentation we held were the documents released on Monday which the amicus questioned the witness about. So I will make sure that's looked into.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, one or two further questions. The list that you have seen on which you are identified with other persons in those indictments and charge sheets, generally, who are the people named in those indictments? Don't name them, just say generally what type of person is named.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In respect of all these charge sheets and criminal reports in all these cases, more or less the same persons are involved. These are primarily the top people of the civilian authorities of the free territory of Brcko. Then there is the entire command of the 108th Brigade, then people from the state security service, and perhaps I can put it this way too, an occasional individual or two that I do not know. But more or less it involves the same people; the top people of civilian and military authorities of the free territory of Brcko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These persons are of Bosniak and Croat ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, Mr. Ramic, your reaction when you heard that you had been given a pardon was what?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've just said. I was very upset. I phoned this judge and I asked quite simply to stop all of this, and I asked where all of this came from, and he told me that he had no other legal possibility other than doing what he had already done, namely amnesty. However, I did address an official request in writing to this court, stating that I refuse this amnesty and that I wanted this invented process to be terminated altogether and annulled.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Pack, perhaps you could find out too whether the amnesty or the pardon, was that in relation to the same charges for which there was a conviction and a judgement. I'm a little confused.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I will find that out. It seems to me I have not seen the -- well, I've seen them very briefly, the documents that the accused produced. It looks like they all date in chronological order from the charge sheets to the indictment to the judgement. And it looks like the amnesty was dated sometime after that, but I will certainly check that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And Mr. Tapuskovic. Mr. Tapuskovic, could you help me with this: In relation to the document produced by the accused which was a judgement and which obviously it seemed to me would have resulted from a trial and a judgement in absentia, firstly, I take it that there is provision in Republika Srpska for a trial in absentia, but what I wanted to ask you was whether one can proceed to a trial in absentia without attempting to enforce the indictment. Can you just proceed straight to a trial in absentia without attempting to serve the indictment on the accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to the laws that were in force throughout this territory at that time, and at that time they were practically applied in the entire territory in spite of the situation, first of all, the court of law would have to do everything possible in order to make sure that the accused person is present, primarily to have the indictment served upon the person involved. And if that does not succeed, then this person is summoned to trial. And if that does not succeed, then a trial can be held in absentia. Then a judgement is reached. If the accused person ever appears before the court of law afterwards, then there has to be retrial. And if we see that there is a judgement that was passed, and we do see that there was a judgement that was passed, then the trial would have to take place all over again. That is in accordance with SFRY regulations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honour may be assisted by asking the witness a few questions about the jurisdiction of the court in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Briefly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just so far as you're aware, Mr. Ramic, the court in Brcko, the present court, the Brcko District Court, did that inherit all proceedings that had been issued under the jurisdiction of the Serb court in Brcko during the war?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Precisely during this conversation that I've already referred to with this judge from that court, the question was raised of how they could amnesty persons involved in proceedings that were conducted by this - how should I put it? - war court of Republika Srpska. The answer I got was that the administration of the district of Brcko legally inherited all previous legal enactments and processes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps the legal officer would come up. Mr. Nice, you can help us about Brcko. I don't want to prolong this, but at some stage we need bringing up-to-date as the present state there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think it is under separate administration, but we will ensure the position is before you with dates of relevant decisions about it. I've seen the material recently. I'll look into it over the break. You presumably would like it in evidential form rather than just from the counsel's role.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I think if counsel would tell us and then if there is any argument about it, we can get it in evidential form.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll get a swift chronology prepared and make it available to you by the next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It can't be a matter of reasonable debate. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Staying with Brcko and the last witness there was the question of the late disclosure or later than usual disclosure of Rule 68 material. As the Chamber knows, the duty of disclosing under Rule 68 imposed by the Rules involves a great deal of material that we have to produce to the accused and we do so. We then produce material that is witness specific shortly before the witness comes because it's much more helpful for him and it also means that we don't produce Rule 68 material for witnesses who in any event don't come which would simply burden him more. In this case it happened that the material to be disclosed to him Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. fell for review a little later than usual. Whether this was a hangover from the holiday period or not, I'm not sure, and he got that bundle of material he revealed to you on the day before, which was later than usual. His cross-examination reveals that the material we provided to him was similar to but in a sense weaker than the material that he had himself because although we haven't been able to compare them, it looks as though the indictments and so on that he produced, which are not available to us, are simply the successor documents to the charge sheets that we were able to produce. So in reality he was not inconvenienced or prejudiced in any way but of course we will do all we can to ensure that the flow of 68 material to the accused goes a sufficient number of days before the witnesses come to give evidence to help him in his preparation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, at present your practice, the practice of the Prosecutor is to search all documents that it has to see whether it has any Rule 68 material.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. If you remember, the overall 68 regime has been described in our several reports, and what we have done is identify a series of search criteria that we apply, and as the Chamber will recall, we regularly remind the Chamber and the amicus and the accused of what the search criteria are so that if they think there's variation that's required, we can consider it and apply it. In addition to that, when any witness comes to give evidence, his name is searched generally within the system. That produces, depending on the witness, a small to enormous amount of material which was then retrieved, printed in hard copy form normally, reviewed by lawyers to see which items within that material qualify for Rule 68 disclosure. Now, there may well be, and I think probably frequently is, an overlap between what is 68 for a specific witness and what will already have been disclosed as part of the general exercise of looking for exculpatory material. But regardless of that, when a witness is coming to give evidence, we search the material, produce what has to be produced for us to review and hand over shortly before the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. I asked the question because I have been developing a view that Rule 68 does not necessarily achieve fairness for all the parties. I believe it is impracticable and unduly onerous. My own view is that it needs to be looked at, to be reviewed and revised so that it is more practicable without doing an injustice to the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm interested to hear those views, and I know that the matter is under general consideration, consideration to which the Office of the Prosecutor is making its contribution. But until there is any change in the Rule, we have to comply with the Rule as it operates on us. Can I turn then to the position with respect to General Van Baal, because the accused drew to your attention that he was provided with some material later again than I would have preferred. In his position, several binders worth of material were identified as needing review, or at least a binder or so, some 130 documents. For internal reasons that I needn't trouble you with, they fell for review later than one would normally have desired. Some 15 documents were identified as needing to be disclosed and one additional one was identified last night, making 16 documents in all, and I hold up the quantity of material in my hand that was disclosed to the accused. It's a combination of press reports, Sitreps of the kind with which the Chamber will be familiar and other documentation. It is not a particularly dense or slow read although, of course, it is documentation that I would have preferred the accused to have had earlier than yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us hear the witness in chief, then begin the cross-examination, and we will see if any issues arise. We will have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, while the witness is coming in, two things. You will see that I am joined today by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Does the Registry have a point? We are told the witness, Mr. Nice, will be giving evidence with interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I should have mentioned that, yes. He speaks what to an English man would be regarded as perfect English, but coming from Holland with a finer tradition of speaking foreign languages he considers there are imperfections and would rather express himself accurately through a Dutch interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours will see that I am joined by Mr. Ierace who has particular experience in the area of Sarajevo and who indeed will be taking some Sarajevo witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If the witness would take the declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, before I forget, although I shan't be referring to it myself, the large map of Sarajevo is available at short notice, providing an easel can be found, should the accused wish to examine, or cross-examine, on any matters of detail.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your full name, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: Van Baal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're a general in the Dutch army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And Your Honour, the witness's testimony in the earlier Galic trial has been admitted subject to the provisions of Rule 92 bis (D) and with cross-examination. In those circumstances, I will read from a summary of the evidence he gave on an earlier occasion, asking him a couple of matters in viva voce evidence and producing one composite exhibit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General Van Baal, I'm about to read a summary of the evidence you gave. I shall attempt to do so at a speed that is suitable and will respond to corrections if I go too fast. This witness was a member of the Dutch army since 1966, chief of UNPROFOR from the 24th of February 1994, and on arrival in Sarajevo in the aftermath of the Markale market incident, sensing that the atmosphere was one of horror where there was an explicit appeal for help. In his judgement there was a centralised and effective command system operating within the VRS which was conducting the battle around Sarajevo through the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, the SRK, whose commander was General Galic, a commander popular with his troops and over whom he had great authority. Galic was subordinate to General Mladic, however, General Milovanovic, chief of the Main Staff of the VRS, also exercised considerable influence over General Galic in day-to-day affairs. The witness was able to confirm contents of a 12th of April, 1994, document which noted that nothing occurs in that region under BSA control without headquarters' knowledge as a result of excellent military discipline. One of the witness's main tasks was to gather or organise the gathering of heavy weapons from the warring factions as part of the total exclusion zone proclamation which was a unilateral decision of NATO to which the warring parties agreed to comply. The total exclusion zone, a circle with a radius of about 20 kilometres centred on Sarajevo, was established by the NATO council and within it heavy weaponry could not be deployed so that it had either to be removed or placed under UNPROFOR control at weapon collection points. Generally the zone was respected and the witness's estimate was that 99 per cent of heavy weapons on the Serb side were placed under the control of Serb forces. However, several weapon systems were removed by the Serb side without permission, were deployed and fired. Further, in the summer of 1994, Serb units made several attempts to remove weapons from a collection point and occasionally or infrequently following application of the agreement, the Serb side did fire heavy weaponry, there being an increase in this use of heavy weaponry after the 5th of August. During the time of his presence in Sarajevo, the witness observed because of the relative success of the total exclusion zone, most destruction occurred in local skirmishes at some points along the confrontation line. As to sniping and following the total exclusion zone agreement, there was initially a sharp reduction in the use of small arms as well as of heavy weaponry by the warring parties. There were sniping incidents which were investigated by the commander of the Sarajevo sector, General Soubirou, carried out under the auspices of the chief UNMO. By March 1994, however, UNPROFOR reports indicated that snipers were being used more actively in Sarajevo, and the witness raised the issue with General Milovanovic at his first meeting with him on the 16th of March in Pale. Milovanovic stated that the trams in Sarajevo should not run until the Serbian bus system was functioning as well and that if UNPROFOR allowed the trams to run, he would see to it that the trams and passengers on them would be targeted. Following that meeting, trams did run, and passengers while on the trams or waiting for them were targeted by snipers so that the witness formed the view that Milovanovic was able to influence sniper activity against trams. In his earlier testimony, the witness was able to read from an UNPROFOR Sitrep of the 3rd of August, 1994, which recorded that on that date at about 1:00 p.m., a sniper operating from a Serbian building shot against a tramway, lightly wounding three Bosnian civilians --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, please read slower. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My apologies. -- also recording the anti-sniper sniping team operating from the Holiday Inn alongside what was known as Sniper Alley returned fire to the sniper. The witness is able to confirm that there were several such incidents in July and August of 1994. He did not know if UNPROFOR anti-sniping teams ever targeted snipers on the Bosnia side as well, but he confirms that there were sniping incidents on both sides. He thought it unlikely that trams would be hit accidently by an exchange of fire along the confrontation line and rejects entirely the suggestion that they were hit by crossfire or ricocheting bullets. In his judgement, the fact that the trams from time to time carried soldiers travelling, other than on active service I suppose, doesn't make it a legitimate military target. One way or another, his opinion is that that doesn't make a legitimate military target of the trams. UNPROFOR started negotiations with the warring parties for an anti-sniping agreement in May of 1994, the agreement being signed in August following an incident on the 14th of August when an 11-year-old child was shot dead on the tram. Both sides claimed they had no control over snipers operating from their respective territories. The sniping from the areas controlled by the Bosnian Serb army was intended and planned to cause terror. The objective was apparent to the witness by their sniping of defenseless citizens, women, children, who were unable to defend or protect themselves at unexpected places and unexpected times. His judgement was that women and children appeared to predominate among civilian casualties. Generals Rose and de la Presle, along with Viktor Andreev, repeatedly and vehemently protested to the VRS leadership about the sniping of civilians in Sarajevo. General Soubirou attempted to protest to General Galic and his liaison officers but following the Gorazde crisis of April 1994, General Mladic forbad contact with UNPROFOR at any level below that of General Van Baal and General Milovanovic, and in particular he wanted no further contact with General Rose, requiring to speak at the level of the four star General de la Presle. Occasionally this witness, General Van Baal, was able to protest orally to the SRK liaison officer, Major Indjic, about the deliberate and indiscriminate shelling and sniping of civilians in Sarajevo from the VRS side of confrontation lines. The responses from both Indjic and Milovanovic varied from a denial that they could control snipers to blaming the enemy for targeting their own civilians. In his prior testimony, the witness read from a document generated by the UNMO, the military observer mission of the United Nations, for the 13th of July of 1994 which noted that on the 12th of July, the commander of the 1st Battalion of the Bosnian Serb army Ilidza Brigade had admitted sniping by that army from a location known as "the house for the blind people." On the topic of proportionality, the witness expressed the view that the use of Serb artillery to neutralise one sniper operating from a room or indeed a sniper's nest in an apartment block where there may have been civilians was disproportionate as use of force. The way to deal with snipers was by snipers. Further, after proclamation of the total exclusion zone, the conflict was minimised so that, for example and in respect of proportionality, an attack on Bosnian positions in Marsal Tito barracks in Sarajevo could no longer be justified. Further, the heavy weapons of the Bosnian army were controlled by UNPROFOR with the exception of possibly a very sporadically used 120-millimetre mortar operating from the vicinity of the airport and possibly in respect of tank fire from near the Kosevo hospital at Serb positions. He had serious doubts that a factory making uniforms could be a legitimate target, but I think he'll probably express his opinion more strongly than that if pressed on it. A command centre in the city on a lower or ground floor in the judgement of the witness could be targeted legitimately with artillery or mortars if no civilians were present in the building. As to the airport, on several occasions Bosnian forces at Butimir used small-arms fire on approaching and departing planes, consequently closing the airport for periods of time. The witness's evidence included that at the end of March 1994, General Mladic urged repeatedly that a cease-fire be imposed throughout Herzegovina, Bosnia-Herzegovina, on condition that the safe areas including Sarajevo be demilitarised. Turning to what that would involve, what military presence there was that would need to be Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. demilitarised, the witness observed in the evidence that there were a large number of military installations in Sarajevo including mobile targets such as military trucks, and he had heard of rumours of a weapons workshop in Marsal Tito barracks but I think nothing more than a rumour. Your Honours, can I turn to the production of the one exhibit through the witness which I trust Your Honours have. The transcript of his evidence, I think, should perhaps be the first tab in his exhibit and then the composite three-part document the second tab.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number 534.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In error I read that the witness was the chief of UNPROFOR. He was the Chief of Staff of the UNPROFOR. I am grateful to Mr. Ierace for seeing that I misread that. And in the Exhibit 524 [sic], we look, please, at tab 2 as I think it is then. You see a three-part composite document, the first being an outgoing table dated the 8th of August, part of the total exclusion zone agreement and dealing with how Serbs were to have access to their impounded weapons particular purposes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that correct, General?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The second page sets out the points of agreement of the total exclusion zone agreement. It can be read at leisure if necessary but under point 1, there was to be unrestricted movement of UNPROFOR verification patrols where possible with a BSA liaison officer. And if we turn to the third sheet, to the protocol of understanding between the civilian military representatives of the Republika Srpska and UNPROFOR, we see at item 4 that at the heart of this agreement really was that neither the Serb nor the Muslim side should be permitted to engage in military activities of any description, this including even the consolidation of trenches or their forward movement or similar activities. Is that correct, General?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One piece of oral evidence from you if you would be so good or -- yes. On the 20th of March, 1994, General, did you receive a report to the effect that there were remote controlled mines placed under Canadian Battalion armoured personnel carriers, and as a result of that did you seek a meeting with Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: I received an oral report, no written report, but the information is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Following your initial approach, did you understand that the mines were removed but did you find that they'd then been repositioned under another armoured personnel carrier and did that lead to your going to Pale on the 21st of March there to meet Karadzic and Galic?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You approached Karadzic and asked for resolution of the problem. Can you summarise, please, his response and apparent authority?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: He recognised that the heavy weapons close to Sertici would be -- that had been positioned within the 20 kilometre perimeter and assigned General Galic to bring those weapons outside the total exclusion zone in the direction of Visoko about 800 metres in north-western direction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's the heavy weapons that needed to be moved. Did Galic appear to agree with Karadzic or not, and if so, how was that disagreement resolved?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: Galic indicated that by moving the heavy weapons, they would be in visual range of the town of Visoko where the Muslim army was positioned, and that would be a vulnerable position. Galic was told to move the weapons anyway, to dig them in, to make them less vulnerable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this was, of course, movement of weapons in accordance with the total exclusion zone agreement which needed some time to take effect; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: That's correct. These weapons were only moved -- were only discovered long after the establishment of the total exclusion zone. First it was attempted to remove those weapons and then on 19 March, General Rose ordered to put the weapons under the control of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As to the mines that you understood had been placed under the Armed Personnel Carrier, how was that resolved at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: This was the second occasion that armed personnel carriers were provided with mines. Mr. Karadzic expressed his amazement to General Galic. He had expected that after the previous night's orders these mines would have been removed from below the APCs. I told him that it was confirmed that the mines were still there. Then he ordered Galic to make sure that the mines were removed from under the APCs. And after some time it was reported both by General Galic and through my contacts in Sarajevo that the mines had been removed from below the APCs of the Canadian Battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this meeting, what Karadzic did and how Galic responded convinced you of what in respect of the existence of command and control at a centralised level?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: First of all, Galic accepted the orders from Karadzic. Secondly, he made sure that by his command and control system he could be informed at a soon -- soon that the mines had been removed from below the APCs. That was only possible if there was an exact execution of the orders and the communication system, a technical communication system that enabled him to hear from Bosnia-Herzegovina what had been done. R

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. You'll be asked some further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Van Baal, as far as I understand, on the 27th of January, 1994, when you were a brigadier general of the Dutch army, you were appointed to duty in Bosnia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: That is not correct. On 24th of February, I went to Bosnia to act as Chief of Staff of --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understood that you had been appointed earlier on but that on the 20th of -- 24th of February you took up your duties officially, took over the duty of Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: I was appointed by the Dutch government on 24th January. I took my position on 24th February.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is precisely what I was asking, General. You were appointed in January and you took over your duties on the 24th of February, 1994. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: I was nominated, and the appointment was done by the UN from 24th February.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that is when you took over your duties and started actively performing those duties as of that date; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: 24th February, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You performed those duties, as far as I can see, up until the 28th of August, 1994. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, General, during the time when you took over these duties and became Chief of Staff, was there a significant shortage of UN officers who were needed to collect intelligence information on the spot?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: There was sufficient personnel, both in Bosnia-Herzegovina command and United Nations military observers to perform the observations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But on page 2, paragraph 6, of your statement, you say that instead of 26 men that had been assigned to collect information, only five were actively working on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness have a copy of his statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct. It has to do with the organisation of the Bosnia-Herzegovina command where expressly it was indicated that it was not mandated to collect military intelligence. Working within the mandate, there was sufficient capacity to collect intelligence and to do investigations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I wanted to clear that up, because that is what it says in the last paragraph of page 1, at least in the Serbian translation. You say that 26 men had been appointed to gather intelligence, but the UN structure did not have the means to accommodate these functions, which meant that in real terms only about five were working.

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: This information in the text is correct. The headquarters of the BH command used to be composed of the structure of the NATO organisation aimed at warfare. In this NATO organisation, 26 persons were planned to do intelligence work. In the context of BH command, these 26 people were not needed because the UN supposed that they were going to be provided with information from the warring sides and it was not necessary to build up their own organisation. That's what I wanted to make clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, then that's very useful as an explanation, General. Does that actually mean that the UN mission, in performing these activities, could not rely exclusively on its own and direct information from the ground but had to utilise other sources of information, as you just mentioned, coming from the warring parties and even using the media as a source?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: Bosnia-Herzegovina's command's mandate was that with collaboration of the parties that had requested us to do our work. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You were under the direct command of General Rose, weren't you, while you were Chief of Staff, throughout your term in office.

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that as the force commander of the UN in Bosnia, he frequently criticised not only the media but other missions too, that they were frequently providing incomplete and very often biased reports from the ground? Incomplete, incorrect, and biased.

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: No comment to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is it right that you're going to call General Rose?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He's on the witness list. As you will appreciate our ability to call -- I'm not ever in a position to undertake absolutely to call witnesses because of the needs to cut witnesses for reasons of time, but he is certainly on the list at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So questions of that sort could more accurately be asked of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, my question related to facts and not to individuals, so I would like to hear the position of General Van Baal about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This diversity of information, since you relied as you yourself say to sources outside the UN mission, did this affect the overall situation on the ground?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: Eventually all information that reaches you has the effect that you form your own opinion. So it must have had an effect. But how sources from outside the mission had an influence to the opinions of General Rose, I cannot judge. He will have to say that by himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But in your own opinion, could you say how sources outside the UN affected your own conclusions?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: I based my opinion on the facts that I recognised that were brought to me through the lines in the Bosnia-Herzegovina command and other source that reported to me, such as UNHCR and --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You performed the post of chief of staff of the mission during a period when the well-known Gorazde crisis occurred and NATO forces acted against the positions of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during your term of office, you had numerous meetings with the highest level representatives of the authorities of the Republika Srpska, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From your statement, I see that your first meeting with the president of the Republika Srpska, Radovan Karadzic, at Pale, took place on the 20th of March.

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It says here that the meeting lasted about three hours. The meeting arose from the following set of circumstances: "General Rose had departed on leave for a week. He left at about 1600 hours. Before he left, we discussed the total exclusion zone and the taking custody of unauthorised heavy weapons close to Visoko," et cetera. So the discussion focused on the overall agreement rather than a particular incident. I gathered from your answer to Mr. Nice's questions that you went there prompted by a particular incident.

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: That's correct. The incident that was discussed before, that is, the item that remote controlled mines under APCs -- had been placed under APCs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you mentioned something else here, General. What it says in this paragraph when you talk about your meeting with the president of Republika Srpska, Dr. Karadzic, that you discussed taking custody of unauthorised heavy weapons in the total exclusion zone near Visoko by members of the Canadian Battalion. So wasn't the content of your three-hour long meeting the question of weapons in the total exclusion zone? You say that the meeting lasted three hours.

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: The meeting took three hours, that's right. It was organised at the occasion of the situation of the previous day where I ordered on behalf of General Rose to the Canadian Battalion to bring the heavy weapons that were in that zone under UNPROFOR and the situation that was created because the Serbian forces of the Ilijas Brigade threatened the Canadian Forces. And the measures that I took then made us decide to address the request of General Karadzic to discuss this in Pale the next day. The immediate occasion was the invitation by Mr. Karadzic to me. Later on that night, we had another contact when it turned out that the remote-controlled mines under -- had been placed under APCs. So the occasion was expressly the threat by the Serb soldiers to UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the transcript, and as I don't understand Dutch, I'm not sure what General Van Baal said, it says that he asked at the request of General Karadzic. That is probably a mistake because he was president of the Republika Srpska, not general. Is it true, General, that the total exclusion zone covered an area of 20 kilometres radius from the centre of the town of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: That's correct, with the centre being a coordinate that had been established in the decision of the NATO council from where the circle had Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to be drawn with a radius of 20 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will adjourn now. General, we're going to adjourn now. One of the usual adjournments. We will break for 20 minutes. I must warn you formally, as we warn all witnesses, not to speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over, and that does include the members of the Prosecution team. Could you be back, please, in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, you speak about these mines. The information I have shows that it was the artillery pieces of the army of Republika Srpska that were mined in case they fall into Serb hands, not the transporters of the Canadian Battalion. Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, Bosnian hands.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is not correct. The Canadian Battalion, without using their weapons and heavy weapons from the Serb army, the Bosnian Serb army were impounded, seized. There was -- this was without any fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that, but it was my understanding on the basis of the information I have that these artillery pieces had been mined, the ones that were left behind by the army of Republika Srpska, not the APCs of the Canadian Battalion. Am I right or not?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: I cannot confirm or deny that. I didn't have the opportunity to personally see where the mines were placed under the artillery of the Serb forces. What I do know what was reported and confirmed to me from several sources is that Serb soldiers from the Ilijas Brigade told the Canadian soldiers to be -- to remain in their own vehicles for their own safety and told them there were remote-controlled mines. That was reported to me from several sources.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I assume not the APCs but underneath the equipment of the army of Republika Srpska. Is that right, General?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's not what the witness has said. You should listen to what he says.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you talked about this particular site where weapons were, the representatives of Republika Srpska then claimed that their weapons were outside the total exclusion zone or on its very outskirts, to be quite precise; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic showed me on a Russian map where, according to him, the total exclusion zone indicated that the arms were within the total exclusion zone. The centre of this circle was assumed to be the historic centre of Sarajevo. This was not what was at hand because the total exclusion zone had been imposed by the NATO council based on a coordinate that was 800 metres from the point where Karadzic had drawn the circle. This caused the weapons to be at a distance of 800 metres from the perimeter of the total exclusion zone, but they were within the total exclusion zone. They were in several locations in the presence of Serb soldiers and global positioning measurements confirmed this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, General, as far as I understand this, the difference was involved in the following: Since we are talking about a 20-kilometre zone, it amounted to 800 metres. So there was differences between the maps, the Russian map shown by Karadzic and your GPS. That's where the difference was; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: The difference was not in the maps but in the fact that the total exclusion zone had been declared and both parties had agreed to the regime, and the centre -- it was not depend on the map used by the parts, but it was imposed by the NATO council. That was the point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. All right. It was my understanding that these were a few pieces of equipment that were within this 800 metres. Were there any targets engaged in Sarajevo and in the surrounding area from that particular area, from those pieces of equipment at that time?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: That was not at hand. Within the 20-kilometre radius, there were not authorised weapons systems that were not under the control of UNPROFOR. That was a point of dispute. That was true for all weapons systems, whether they were within 800 metres or not from the perimeters, all systems within the 20-kilometre radius.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that. My question was whether these pieces of equipment, these weapons that happened to be within these 800 metres were used to engage targets. Did anybody shoot from these weapons?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: The point was not if they were used but if they could be used. They could be moved besides. They -- after they had been put at a weapon collection point, they were under the responsibility of the Ilijas Brigade, and they could be moved and deployed at any time. So it was -- we wanted to remove them from the total exclusion zone because it was contrary to our agreement. That was the point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. All right. I understand that that was the point, to remove them from the total exclusion zone, but at that time when the agreement was enforced, these weapons were not used for shooting at all, although they were within those 800 metres. Is that right, General?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: It is not the point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But was there any shooting coming from these weapons?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: At any rate, from the time we discovered them, that was only late in March, they were under control. UNMO inspected them regularly, also to discuss the removal of these weapons. In that period, we could not find any use of those weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. So on the 20th of March at 1730 hours, you took control over this weaponry and then you say you were surrounded by a unit of the army of Republika Srpska consisting of about 600 men from the Ilijas Brigade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: Not immediately at 1530 hours, only later in the afternoon this took place that the Serb -- Bosnian Serb Ilijas Brigade in large numbers surrounded the Canadian brigade. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But you yourself say on page 4, in paragraph 2, you say: "At 1730 hours, the Canadians went with 45 APCs to the unauthorised weapons near Visoko and brought the heavy weapons under control. Then they found themselves surrounded by approximately 600 Bosnian Serbs, VRS soldiers from the Ilijas Brigade," and so on and so forth. So that means that then at 1730 hours, you did place these weapons under your control. Is that right, General?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when they surrounded you, did any soldier of Republika Srpska open fire at your men? Was there any incident of this nature involved? Were any of your men injured or was there any kind of conflict that they had caused?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: No weapons were used by the Serb soldiers. There was a threat that from 1930 hours fire would be opened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Your first contact with Karadzic was over the telephone then after that particular event. And then you say that after that, he issued an order for the withdrawal of the soldiers of Republika Srpska from that position, and that was indeed done within 15 or 20 minutes; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 4 in paragraph 4, you say that this was a clear indicator to you that the army of Republika Srpska had a very centralised command and control structure and excellent communications. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you had contact with the president of Republika Srpska, and you asked him to have the soldiers of the army of Republika Srpska withdrawn, and he acted exactly the way you wanted him to. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you say that the command and control structure was very centralised. Was it more or less centralised than that in any other army in the world? Isn't that customary for an order to be carried out once it is issued by the Supreme Commander? Isn't that logical?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: It is logical.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement, on page 4, paragraph 4, you say that the members of the Canadian Battalion in the field, after the withdrawal of the Serb forces, discovered that the Serbs had laid remote-controlled mines under some of the APCs. Some of the APCs you say.

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that means, since you had control over these pieces of equipment, that this had been done earlier, because soldiers of the army of Republika Srpska did not have access to these pieces of equipment after you had taken them over. Isn't that right, General?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: Whether they had access or not, let's leave that now, but I can only say that we got a report that Serb soldiers had approached the Canadian forces in the dark and for their own safety they impressed upon them to stay in their vehicles and not to stay outside and for a number of reasons. The Canadian soldiers followed this advice. When in the night these soldiers went outside, they discovered that under their APCs there were remote-controlled mines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was my understanding that they had been laid underneath these particular pieces of equipment, the APCs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have been round and round this point, and I don't think we're going to get any further. We have the witness's evidence on it. Let's move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The meeting you had with Radovan Karadzic on that occasion was conducted in the presence of General Galic, the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that Karadzic at one point in time said to Galic that he had promised him that these explosive devices would be removed as early as the previous night?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you say in paragraph 4, on page 5 that Galic, although according to your impression, did not like that order of Karadzic's acted in accordance with the order issued by his president. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: In first instance that happened during the night, but in the early morning, there were remote-controlled mines put under the APCs of the Canadian Forces, and they were still there when I arrived in Pale around 10.00 a.m. Then I requested again to remove the -- to -- I reported again that remote-controlled mines had been put under the APCs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it was then that this dialogue took place, the one that I quoted to you only a short while ago that you refer to when Karadzic asked for the mines to be removed, the ones that you had talked about, and that this was indeed carried out?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: At the second occasion, Galic performed the orders of Karadzic to remove the mines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. On page 6, in paragraph 2, you say that when you met with the Muslim side, you held meetings with General Divjak, although in your opinion he did not have any power. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, although you knew this, why did you meet with a person who did not have any power? Wasn't that a waste of time?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: It was the only contact that I was allowed. General Delic did not want to talk to General Rose or to me, and Milanovic and Hasanovic were not available, so I used the office to -- the offer to talk to General Divjak, and he would pass on the conversation to the other generals I just mentioned, and he could not take any decisions on the issues I wanted to discuss with him. Did he not have the authority. I immediately noticed that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you held with meetings -- but you did hold meetings both with Hadzihasanovic and Halilovic; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: A number of times I spoke to Hasanovic and Halilovic, that's correct, but they were not always available. That's why I used the contact with General Divjak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And what about the two of them, Hadzihasanovic and Halilovic, were they persons of authority, persons who did have certain powers?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: I noticed that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was authorised on the Muslim side to carry out relevant negotiations and to reach decisions? Can you say that?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: In general, that was General Delic and Halilovic and Hadzihasanovic also.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. On page 6, in paragraph 3, you say that you encountered Fikret Abdic in connection with the situation and the war operations in Bihac. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that he did not want to cooperate then with the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina and if so, do you know why not?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: After my observations during the conversation, I noticed he had no wish to have any contact with the central government in Sarajevo. He didn't trust them. And he very much relied on his own strength and his own coalition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And do you know that your commander, General Rose, together with Ejub Ganic also visited Bihac and had contacts with Abdic but also with Atif Dudakovic, commander of the 5th Corps who was immediately involved in the war operations there?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: I don't know what particular time you're referring to, and it's not clear to me which visit particularly you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know of the visits of General Rose to this Bihac region together with Ejub Ganic and contacts with Atif Dudakovic, commander of the 5th Corps of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: The visit of General Rose's is still clear to me. Whether Mr. Ganic joined General Rose or not, I cannot remember. I do know that General Rose, before I left for Bihac, met General Dudakovic and Mr. Abdic and talked with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, General, do you agree with the assessment made by Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. General Rose that he presented, and I'm going to quote it, he makes the following comment with regarding his meeting with Dudakovic. He says: "I knew this strategy of his from earlier on because it did not differ from the way in which the Muslim army operated in any part of the territory. First of all, attacks around their own positions, then withdrawing into the exclusion zone protesting about the suffering of the population, and thirdly, calls upon NATO and the UN to bomb the Serbs." Do you agree with this assessment of his?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: I can't ascertain whether that is a quote of General Rose's or not, and I leave that for General Rose to say. I have no comment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I can quote this from his book, page 127, paragraph 4. He says: "I knew that strategy of his from earlier on because it did not differ from the way the Muslim army operated in any part of the territory. "Number one, attack --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You have read that out and the witness has given you the answer that he has no comment on it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about your own experience, which was shorter, of course, considerably shorter from the experience of your commander, General Rose? Does it point to the same thing regarding the general strategy of the Muslim forces throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: My experience is that all parties in the conflict have tried to make the Bosnia-Herzegovina command do what they wanted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's the UNPROFOR command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. From my situation, it was the Bosnia-Herzegovina command, which is part of UNPROFOR in total. That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that the French Colonel Legrier [phoen] sent information to the effect that light Croatian aircraft were often violating the no-fly zone and delivering weapons to Dudakovic's 5th Corps? Do you know about that fact? General Rose refers to that too, so I assume that you are aware of it as well.

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: During my period of office, there was some -- there was some mention that small aircraft and fixed-wing aircraft and helicopters without authorisation were flying over the Bosnia-Herzegovina territory. This was reported to us through NATO channels, but we couldn't confirm. And if General Rose can say something about that with certainty, he must have had the information. I myself was never able to confirm that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that on the 1st of April, 1994, Alija Izetbegovic called early in the morning, at 2.30 a.m., General Rose and said to him that there were tanks in the streets of Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that as far as a specific telephone conversation is concerned. But I do know that in the run-up to the Gorazde crisis there was regular contact between General Rose and the Muslim government in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you know that General Rose was asked - Alija Izetbegovic asked him, as a matter of fact - to have NATO intervention, air intervention, against Serb-held positions because they were present in the zone that was off limits? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: That's right. During the Gorazde crisis, I [as interpreted] regularly insisted that according to the UN Security Resolution 863 rules, the secure zone of Gorazde should be protected in the last resort by air power if need be, airstrikes or close-air support. The Bosnian Muslim authorities repeatedly insisted on this happening throughout the crisis, that's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is this assessment of General Rose's correct, the one that has to do with the following: "My previous experience pointed to the fact that these were exaggerations and that the Muslim requests contained overexaggerations concerning their losses. I called General Leavitt nevertheless and asked him what the latest intelligence was, and he said to me that the pressure against Bosnian forces from Gorazde was no doubt continuing but that there was no other alarming information." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: The information I had as Chief of Staff was based on observations by MSF and UNHCR representatives in the centre of Gorazde. And from that reporting, it was abundantly clear that tank and artillery fire had been shot at the hospital, among others, in Gorazde, and also that shells had impacted in the town of Gorazde itself. That was a confirmation I received from the PTT building in Gorazde where the observers were. So in my opinion, there was enormous pressure on the town, and there was the use of heavy weapons. And after the event, it appeared there were about 300 casualties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One matter I'm going to raise while it's on the monitors. The witness's answer before last about the Gorazde crisis, the transcript has it, "I regularly insisted that according to the resolution the secure zone of Gorazde should be protected in the last resort by airstrikes." My recollection is that the witness said it was President Izetbegovic who regularly insisted that according to the resolution, et cetera, in the last resort by airstrikes. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's page 84, line 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, General, is it true that Izetbegovic's call and information at the time was incorrect and desired exclusively to ensure NATO strikes on Serb positions?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: I did not base my opinion on the telephone conversations of the Muslim leaders in Sarajevo but on the reports I received from Gorazde itself. As to the exact content of the conversations between Muslim leaders and General Rose, I don't know. I do know that General Rose told me that the Muslim authorities insisted on the deployment of NATO air force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Is it also true - and this is on page 6, paragraph 3 of your statement - that you said that you attended a meeting with Mladic and Delic, and at that meeting Mladic proposed a general cease-fire throughout the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina and not just in Gorazde. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: That is right. This was in the run-up to the Gorazde crisis in the period March 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true that Delic rejected this, that is, Mladic's proposal for a total cease-fire in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: That's true. General Delic was primarily interested in stopping the fighting and the skirmishes around Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the cessation of all activities meant also a cessation of activities around Gorazde, didn't it? And Delic would not accept this. He just asked for activities to cease around Gorazde without accepting a complete cease-fire for Bosnia and Herzegovina as a whole. Is that right, General?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: It's partly right, because General Mladic attached a condition to it, i.e., demilitarisation of all military in the safe areas Tuzla, Srebrenica, Gorazde, Bihac --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Witness mentioned a few more.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and this, as far as the general was concerned, was not to be discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that a logical requirement? A total cease-fire, a demilitarisation of the safe areas, which would mean security for all, a cease-fire throughout the territory and a demilitarisation of the safe areas. Of course, that do not include the UN which was present there.

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: It was a unilateral demilitarisation of the areas where Bosnian Muslims were in power. It would have meant complete surrender of the Bosnian Muslim army. And as far as Delic was concerned, that was not acceptable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those were protected areas, safe areas. Your forces were there, which the Serbs never attacked. Isn't that right, General?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: They were secure areas, that is true, but I'm not saying what my opinion is. The opinion of Mr. Galic is what I reported because that's what you were asking. And it was about the fact -- it says General Delic, begging your pardon - that he could not accept these conditions because, as he saw it, that meant demob'ing the entire Bosnian Muslim army, and that would have meant a total surrender. That was his position, and that's why he didn't want to discuss it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that General Delic, on the 7th of April, requested first a complete political agreement on the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and only after that could a cessation of hostilities throughout the territory be discussed?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: I cannot remember whether General Delic went into proposals as specifically as that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Michael Rose says in his book: "Delic demanded that full political agreement be reached before military negotiations start on a cease-fire."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has given his recollection of these matters, and I don't think there's much point putting what somebody else says about it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The witness also says that Delic, as far as I understand it, wanted a political agreement to be reached first. Can one conclude from that that the Muslim side was not interested in a cease-fire but primarily in a division of territory before a cease-fire was reached?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: For General Delic, what was important in the negotiations under the leadership of General Rose, that what was happening around Gorazde would stop before he was even interested in a total cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. But at the time, you were Chief of Staff, and General Rose says for that time period that the message of UNMO officers seemed as if they had been dictated of the Muslim authorities from Gorazde, because they were contrary to everything that the press spokesman of the United Nations stated in Sarajevo. The Serbs never even tried to take control of that town. Does that concur with your own knowledge, General, or not?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: My knowledge of that period is that General Rose relied more on his own people in Gorazde, his British military, than UNMO officers there. I had no direct access to his British military but to UNMOs and the MSF and UNHCR staff, and I based my opinion on that. What I did notice myself during my visit later to Gorazde, a couple of weeks later, is that there were still clear traces of hostilities and that there were tanks on the edge of Gorazde. The -- I'm sure the intention was not to take in the city with its 30.000 refugees, but there was fighting in its periphery and in the city itself, and it was shot at by tanks and artillery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true, General, that about that time there were frequent incidents or, rather, attacks by Muslim forces coming from Gorazde outside the safe area and targeting many Serb villages east of the Drina River? Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: ADRIANUS VAN BAAL
utterances.text: At at least two points, General Milovanovic told me that Bosnian Muslim military were -- or had shot at military and civilians. He'd wounded them and killed them. General Milovanovic told me that twice, but I wasn't able to ascertain that myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
